About this citation

The aphorism numbers are the locator, and they are stable. Section 341 is the eternal-recurrence question; §276 is the line about wanting to learn nothing new anymore. The 1887 edition added a fifth book, so the year attached to an aphorism matters for which collection it sits in.

### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Amor fati: let that be my love from now on!”

Latin

“Amor fati.”

Latin, coined as a phrase rather than quoted from an earlier author. The German sentence it sits in is “Amor fati: das sei von nun an meine Liebe!”

### Attribution notes

“Amor fati” is Nietzsche's own formulation in The Gay Science §276 — it is not a Stoic term of art, however frequently it is filed under Stoicism. Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius counsel acceptance of what is not in our control; Nietzsche's love of fate also wills that the past have been exactly as it was, which is a heavier demand and connects to the eternal recurrence shortly after.

#### About Friedrich Nietzsche

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German classical philologist who became a radical critic of morality, metaphysics, and modern culture. Appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four, he resigned from ill health and wrote in solitude across Switzerland, Italy, and Germany.

### How to read this passage

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Epictetus and Seneca), fate is framed through Stoicism and Philosophy of Will. Some passages define fate; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through fate, affirmation.
